chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
title: Columbia Studios music department: Stoller and Bakaleinikoff
summary: Lee describes Morris Stoll and Misha Bakaleinikoff at Columbia, and the practice of reusing music, which was banned in 1977.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: But anyway, we -- I went to the studio, and Bachalenakoff, who was ...
So Misha was at Columbia, but Misha was not the first man. Morris Stoller was the head of the music department and he was number one conductor there. He did all the biggies there.

But Misha Bachalenkakoff, he did all of the 'B' things; at that time, you could take music from the A pictures that were done, and edit them down and get your main title and get your end title and get your chase music and get whatever you had to do, and Misha was a genius at doing that. He would look at the picture and he would put the music to it, so then that would mean that they wouldn't have to record any more music, but that rule is out now. You know, as a matter of fact, this year -- 1977 -- they just passed a rule that you can't put anything in the can, you know, you can't go and get it. Once you've used it, that's it; you have to record fresh again.
So that's a great rule for the musicians, you know, and I think it's a fair thing. But anyway, going to work at Columbia and being on the staff, you know, it was quite

an honor; for a white musician or a black musician; whatever you were -- that was really steady. You didn't have to worry about where you were gonna get work; you pick up your check every week, and it was considered the best job in town to be on the staff.
